screens.title: Reentrancy Attacks & Prevention
screens.subtitle: How external calls and state order create a critical vulnerability — and how to defend against it

narration.text: In this lesson you'll build a deep, practical understanding of reentrancy: what causes it, how attackers exploit it, and the proven code patterns that stop it. We'll begin with the historic context that shaped modern smart contract defenses, then examine the exact sequence of actions that allows an attacker to re-enter a function while its state is inconsistent. You will see a vulnerable withdraw example and a secure refactor that follows the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern. We'll also cover the practical use of reentrancy guards supplied by libraries like OpenZeppelin, and why the low-level call primitive requires careful handling. Throughout, you'll get concrete advice about transfer, send, and call, including their gas behaviors and trade-offs. By the end of the module you will know how to spot vulnerable patterns in code reviews, apply CEI consistently, and add a nonReentrant lock when needed. Think of this as a toolkit: correct state ordering first, then safe external calls, and finally defensive mutexes when complexity demands it. Keep an eye out for the common mistaken belief that transfer alone is a full solution — it's a useful mitigation but not a universal fix.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Reentrancy happens when an external call allows the callee to call back into the original function before state updates complete. Prevent it by updating state before external calls (CEI) and using reentrancy guards when needed.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain exactly how a reentrancy attack is executed, identify the vulnerable code pattern where state is changed after an external call, and refactor such code to obey the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern. You will also know how to use OpenZeppelin's ReentrancyGuard and understand when a mutex is necessary. Finally, you'll be able to compare transfer, send, and call in terms of gas forwarding and reentrancy risk, and pick the right tool for your contract's needs. Each objective ties to a practical skill: finding the bug in an audit, fixing a vulnerable withdraw, applying a nonReentrant modifier when appropriate, and choosing an Ether transfer method that balances safety and compatibility. These skills reduce the chance of catastrophic fund loss and make your contracts resilient in composable DeFi environments. We'll reinforce these with code examples and a small lab where you refactor a vulnerable Bank contract and test an attacker contract locally.

screens.title: How we will practice
screens.subtitle: Refactor, inherit, and test a vulnerable withdraw flow

narration.text: This second objectives slide maps to a hands-on workflow. You will start from a minimal vulnerable Bank contract, add deposits, then reproduce an attack with an attacker contract to see the exploit in action. Next you'll refactor the withdraw function to follow Checks-Effects-Interactions, then inherit OpenZeppelin's ReentrancyGuard and apply nonReentrant. Finally, you will deploy both SafeBank and the Attacker locally or in Remix and confirm the attack fails. Practicing this sequence helps you internalize the defensive ordering and the role of a mutex in complex flows. The activity forces you to reason about gas limits, call behavior, and legitimate contract recipients that might need more gas. That tension explains why modern best practice is to use call with CEI and a reentrancy guard rather than relying purely on transfer. After running the attack and the defended contract you'll be able to justify your chosen mitigation in a code review and explain residual risks such as oracle trust assumptions.

screens.title: History: The DAO exploit and why reentrancy matters
screens.subtitle: Real-world consequences that shaped security thinking

narration.text: The DAO exploit is a vivid, real-world reason why reentrancy matters. In that case, an attacker used a reentrant call path to repeatedly withdraw funds before the contract could update accounting, causing a massive loss of Ether and triggering a network response. The lesson is structural: when a contract trusts that its state remains constant across an external call, that assumption can be violated if the recipient is able to call back. That failure mode isn't just a theoretical bug; it led to one of the earliest, largest governance decisions in the ecosystem. Understanding that sequence helps you audit contracts with the right mental model. When you review code, look for patterns where funds or critical counters are adjusted only after an external call — those are high risk. Also consider subtle variations: reentrancy can appear in token callbacks or more complex state machines, not just in simple withdraw functions. A misconception to watch for is believing reentrancy only matters for large contracts. In reality, any contract that holds or routes funds or that relies on consistent counters is susceptible. The practical takeaway is to treat every external call as untrusted and structure your code so state reflects pending actions before giving control away.

keyIdea.title: Historical lesson
keyIdea.text: The DAO exploit shows how reentrancy can drain funds when state is updated after an external call; treat external calls as untrusted.

screens.title: What is a reentrancy attack?
screens.subtitle: Precise mechanics and the vulnerable call pattern

narration.text: A reentrancy attack happens when a contract makes an external call and the callee is able to call back into the original contract before that original function completes its state updates. Concretely, the vulnerable pattern commonly looks like: check balance, make external call to the caller, then update the balance after the call. Because the external call transfers control to potentially untrusted code, that code can call the withdraw function again. The second call sees the original balance still in place, so the require check passes again, and funds are drained through repetition. A clear definition helps you watch for the telltale code smell: state mutations coming after interactions. A concrete example is a withdraw function that calls the recipient with call{value: amount} and only then decrements balances. A helpful contrast is reentrancy versus other bugs: reentrancy depends on control flow and external calls, whereas arithmetic overflows are purely internal calculation issues. A common misconception is believing reentrancy only requires a fallback function; in fact it requires the ability to call back into the vulnerable function before state update, which can be achieved via receive or fallback or any callable function in the recipient. The takeaway: treat every external call as a potential entry point and reorder your logic to remove that entry opportunity.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Reentrancy allows an external callee to call back into a function before state changes finish; it arises when interactions happen before effects.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Reentrancy Definition
Reentrancy explained
Vulnerable pattern
Check balance → External call to recipient → Update balance. The external call can re-enter before update.
Concrete example
A withdraw that calls msg.sender.call{value: amount}("") before decrementing balances allows repeated withdrawals.
Contrast
Reentrancy is about control flow and external interactions. It is distinct from arithmetic or access control bugs.
Key takeaway
Always assume external calls are untrusted and order state updates before making them.

screens.title: Vulnerable withdraw example
screens.subtitle: Read the code that enables repeated withdrawals

narration.text: Let's walk through a minimal vulnerable withdraw implementation to make the fault visible. The key lines are the require check, the external call via call with value, and then the balance decrement that happens last. Because the decrement occurs after the external call, a malicious recipient can re-enter by using its receive or fallback and call withdraw again. In practice you'll see the attacker deposit an initial amount, call withdraw, and then the fallback triggers repeated withdrawals until funds are depleted or gas runs out. When you inspect the code pay attention to the ordering: the check is fine, but effects must come before interactions. A common misread is to assume a require prevents re-entry because it validates balances; it does on the first entry, but not on subsequent re-entries if state wasn't updated. When you test this locally, the Attacker contract's receive function will perform a conditional re-call while the Bank's balance hasn't been updated yet. Observing the transaction trace or console logs helps you see the number of nested calls and the point at which funds were drained. The learning task is to reproduce this and then refactor safely.

keyIdea.title: Vulnerable pattern
keyIdea.text: External call before state mutation enables the callee to call back and bypass the intended balance checks repeatedly.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Vulnerable withdraw
Vulnerable withdraw
function withdraw(uint256 _amount) public {
    require(balances[msg.sender] >= _amount, "Insufficient balance");

    // External call BEFORE state update
    (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: _amount}("");
    require(success, "Transfer failed");

    balances[msg.sender] -= _amount;
}
Common mistake
Assuming the require alone stops repeated withdrawals. It does not if state change happens after the call.
Concrete attacker flow
Attacker deposits, calls withdraw, then its receive fallback calls withdraw again while original call hasn't decremented balance.
Key Takeaway
Never make untrusted external calls before updating critical state like balances.

screens.title: Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI) pattern
screens.subtitle: A simple, powerful ordering rule to prevent reentrancy

narration.text: The Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern prescribes a strict ordering: perform all checks first, then apply all state effects, and only then make external interactions. This reduces the attack surface because once the external call executes, the contract's state already reflects the pending operation and a re-entrant call will fail the checks. For a withdraw flow the concrete steps are: first require the caller has enough balance, then subtract the amount from the stored balance, finally perform the external transfer and verify success. That single reordering closes the basic exploit vector shown earlier. It is not a panacea — complex cross-function interactions or multi-step protocols might need additional controls — but CEI should be your first line of defense on any fund-managing function. A common misconception is that CEI is only necessary for transfers; in fact it applies to any external call that can change control flow, including token callbacks. Use CEI consistently and combine it with unit and integration tests that simulate adversarial re-entry to validate your refactor. Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI) pattern means checks first, effects second, interactions last. ordering state updates before external calls prevents basic reentrancy.. In practical terms, a simple, powerful ordering rule to prevent reentrancy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: CEI core
keyIdea.text: Checks first, Effects second, Interactions last. Ordering state updates before external calls prevents basic reentrancy.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Checks-Effects-Interactions
Checks-Effects-Interactions
1. Checks: validate inputs and balances.
2. Effects: update balances and state variables immediately.
3. Interactions: perform external calls last and check results.
Example refactor
function withdrawSafe(uint256 _amount) public {
    require(balances[msg.sender] >= _amount, "Insufficient balance");

    balances[msg.sender] -= _amount; // Effect: update first

    (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: _amount}("");
    require(success, "Transfer failed");
}
Key Takeaway
Reordering stops the simple reentrant loop because repeated require checks fail after the effect step.

narration.text: A reentrancy guard implements a simple mutex: when a guarded function begins executing it flips a status to indicate 'entered' and when it finishes it flips back to 'not entered'. If a reentrant call tries to enter while the status is 'entered', the guard reverts. OpenZeppelin's ReentrancyGuard is a common, well-tested implementation used across many contracts. It integrates cleanly: inherit the guard and mark vulnerable functions with nonReentrant. Guards are particularly useful when a function is complex, spans multiple internal calls, or when maintaining CEI across many functions is difficult. However, guards are not a substitute for good ordering; they are a complementary layer. A common misconception is that adding a mutex removes the need to think about state order — that's false. You should still apply CEI where possible and use guards to catch edge cases or protect public entry points. Another subtlety: a nonReentrant modifier prevents the same guarded function from being re-entered, but it does not prevent re-entry across different functions unless designed to do so. Use the guard intentionally and document which functions are protected. Reentrancy Guard (nonReentrant) means a mutex prevents re-entrant calls during execution. use it as a defensive complement to cei for complex flows.. In practical terms, mutex-based protection provided by libraries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Guard idea
keyIdea.text: A mutex prevents re-entrant calls during execution. Use it as a defensive complement to CEI for complex flows.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Reentrancy Guard
ReentrancyGuard
Concept
A simple mutex flips state on entry and exit. If a reentrant call occurs while locked, it reverts.
When to use it
On public functions that perform transfers or complex state changes where CEI alone is difficult to enforce.
import "@openzeppelin/contracts/security/ReentrancyGuard.sol";

contract SafeBank is ReentrancyGuard {
    mapping(address => uint256) public balances;

    function withdraw(uint256 _amount) public nonReentrant {
        require(balances[msg.sender] >= _amount, "Insufficient balance");
        balances[msg.sender] -= _amount;
        (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: _amount}("");
        require(success, "Transfer failed");
    }
}
Misconception
Mutexes block re-entry for guarded functions but don't replace careful state ordering or design reviews.

narration.text: When sending Ether from a contract you typically choose between transfer, send, and call. Historically transfer and send forwarded a fixed 2300 gas stipend, which limited what the recipient's fallback could do and therefore made reentrancy harder. That limited gas could prevent complex fallback logic and thus block re-entrant calls, but it also caused legitimate recipient contracts that needed more gas to fail. Modern Solidity favors call because it forwards all available gas by default and is more flexible for composability. However call increases reentrancy risk if you don't update state first or use a reentrancy guard. The recommended modern practice is to use call coupled with CEI and nonReentrant when appropriate. A common mistake is to rely on transfer as a universal defense; its gas limit can break valid contracts and does not remove the need for CEI. When choosing a strategy think about compatibility with recipients, the expected complexity of their fallback logic, and whether you can enforce CEI and tests. In many protocols, using call plus a guard gives both flexibility and safety. transfer, send, and call — trade-offs means transfer/send limit gas (2300) and can mitigate reentrancy but may break valid recipients; call is flexible but requires cei and guards.. In practical terms, gas forwarding and reentrancy implications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Transfer trade-offs
keyIdea.text: transfer/send limit gas (2300) and can mitigate reentrancy but may break valid recipients; call is flexible but requires CEI and guards.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › transfer vs send vs call
Choosing a transfer method
transfer()
Forwards 2300 gas, reentrancy-resistant in many cases, but can break receivers that need more gas.
send()
Similar to transfer, returns a boolean on success or failure. Same gas limitation applies.
call()
Forwards all available gas by default. Flexible but requires CEI and guards to be safe.
Practical rule
Prefer call with CEI and a reentrancy guard for maximum compatibility and safety.
Mistake to avoid
Relying solely on transfer for security can cause legitimate transactions to fail and ignores other attack vectors.

screens.title: Refactor: withdrawSafe using CEI
screens.subtitle: A live refactor to update state before interaction

narration.text: Here we refactor the vulnerable withdraw into a safe pattern by moving the state mutation prior to the external call. The critical change is simple but powerful: decrement the balance before performing call. This causes any re-entrant attempt to fail the initial require check on the second invocation. When you implement this change, run unit tests that simulate attacker behavior to ensure the logic holds up under repeated nested calls. Remember that while CEI prevents the basic reentry loop, you should also consider other functions that may call into this flow and enforce consistent ordering across them. Another practical concern: handle failures from call properly by reverting when the transfer fails, and ensure your contract invariants remain consistent on failure paths. A common pitfall is forgetting to emit events or update auxiliary accounting after reordering; verify side effects and external expectations remain correct. The final check is deploying to a local test environment and running the Attacker contract to confirm the refactor closes the exploit. Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › withdrawSafe Refactor
Refactor: CEI applied
function withdrawSafe(uint256 _amount) public {
    require(balances[msg.sender] >= _amount, "Insufficient balance");

    balances[msg.sender] -= _amount; // Effect: Update first

    (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: _amount}("");
    require(success, "Transfer failed");
}
Check
Run attacker tests to ensure nested calls cannot withdraw twice.
Practical note
If transfer fails, your require will revert and the state remains consistent because the effect occurred before the interaction. Confirm desired behavior for failed payments.
Misconception
CEI alone cannot protect across multiple interacting functions unless the same discipline is applied everywhere.

narration.text: A layered defense uses CEI as the primary prevention mechanism and a reentrancy guard as a protective safety net. CEI eliminates the simple reentrant loop by ensuring state shows the pending operation before any external call. The guard then prevents re-entry even when flows are complex or when multiple functions interact. Practically, inherit OpenZeppelin's ReentrancyGuard, mark critical functions nonReentrant, and still apply CEI inside those functions. This combined approach is especially useful for contracts that perform several external interactions or maintain complex invariants across multiple functions. One subtle point is that nonReentrant prevents the same guarded function from being re-entered, so guard design should consider which functions must be mutually exclusive. Also, document why each function is guarded so auditors understand the intended invariants. The layered pattern reduces the chance that a single oversight will become a catastrophic exploit and it simplifies audits because you can reason about both ordering and entry control. Combining CEI with ReentrancyGuard means use cei first and add a mutex guard as a secondary protection, especially in complex or multi-call flows.. In practical terms, layered defenses for robust contracts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Layered defense
keyIdea.text: Use CEI first and add a mutex guard as a secondary protection, especially in complex or multi-call flows.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › CEI + Guard
Combine CEI and nonReentrant
Pattern
Apply CEI inside functions and protect public entry points with a nonReentrant modifier to ensure mutually exclusive execution.
Example
contract SafeBank is ReentrancyGuard {
    mapping(address => uint256) public balances;

    function withdraw(uint256 _amount) public nonReentrant {
        require(balances[msg.sender] >= _amount);
        balances[msg.sender] -= _amount; // CEI effect
        (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: _amount}("");
        require(success);
    }
}
Why it helps
CEI deals with ordering; the guard catches unexpected re-entries or oversights in complex flows.
Design note
Ensure guards cover the right functions and document intended mutual exclusions for future maintainers.

narration.text: The hands-on activity walks you through a lab: start with the provided vulnerable Bank and Attacker contracts. First deploy Bank, then deploy Attacker pointing to Bank's address. If Attacker still manages to drain funds, examine all paths where external calls happen and apply CEI and guards consistently. screens.title: Assessment: reasoning about external calls and oracles
screens.subtitle: A short conceptual quiz and reasoning checks

narration.text: Assessments should test your ability to reason about when reentrancy is a direct risk and when it is not. For example, consider a repayLoan function that first calls an oracle for an exchange rate, then calculates interest, and finally updates a loan balance. This sequence makes the oracle call appear before the state update, but reentrancy requires an untrusted recipient that can call back into the contract's vulnerable function. If the oracle is trusted and does not call back, this setup is not directly vulnerable to reentrancy. However, external calls to untrusted addresses before updating state are a red flag. Another assessment checks understanding of transfer: asking why transfer's fixed gas is not a silver bullet. The correct responses should show you know that transfer limits fallback gas but can break legitimate recipients, and that modern best practice favors call with CEI and guards. Design questions that require explaining a rationale, not just selecting an answer: ask the learner to propose a defensive change and to justify why CEI plus nonReentrant is appropriate or not for a given flow. Assessment: reasoning about external calls and oracles means test reasoning about untrusted external calls, oracle trust, and choosing defenses with proper justification.. In practical terms, a short conceptual quiz and reasoning checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from Reentrancy Attacks & Prevention

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential concepts you should carry forward. First, a reentrancy attack allows an external callee to call back into a contract before state changes complete. Second, the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern is the first-line defense: validate inputs, update state, then interact externally. Third, ReentrancyGuard provides a mutex via a nonReentrant modifier that prevents guarded functions from being called again during execution. Fourth, choose your Ether transfer method with care: transfer and send forward only 2300 gas which can mitigate certain attacks but limit legitimate fallbacks; call is flexible but requires CEI and guard protections. Finally, always treat external calls as untrusted and complement code ordering with tests that simulate attacker behavior. These compact rules make auditing and designing safe fund-handling functions much simpler and reduce the risk of catastrophic loss.

keyIdea.title: Recap
keyIdea.text: Reentrancy is prevented by CEI and reentrancy guards; prefer call with CEI and nonReentrant for compatibility and safety.

Summary takeaway

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders for safe contracts

narration.text: Keep three compact reminders in mind. First, always assume external calls are untrusted and order your code so state reflects pending operations before giving control away. Second, use CEI as your first defense and validate that all code paths follow it, including token callbacks and multi-step flows. Third, add a reentrancy guard as a defensive belt-and-braces approach when functions are complex or exposed as public entry points. Additionally, weigh your transfer choice: transfer and send limit gas but can break legitimate receivers; call plus CEI and guards is the modern, flexible approach. Practice by refactoring a vulnerable withdraw, running the attacker test, and confirming the attack no longer succeeds. These steps will help you design contracts that resist one of the oldest and most damaging classes of attacks. What to Remember means assume external calls are unsafe, apply cei everywhere, and use reentrancy guards for complex flows; prefer call with these defenses.. In practical terms, three compact reminders for safe contracts. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. keyIdea.title: Three reminders
keyIdea.text: Assume external calls are unsafe, apply CEI everywhere, and use reentrancy guards for complex flows; prefer call with these defenses.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › What to Remember
Assume calls are untrusted
Any external call may change control flow; code accordingly.
Apply CEI
Checks, then Effects, then Interactions to remove re-entry windows.
Use guards
Add nonReentrant where complexity or public access increases risk.
Final practice tip
Refactor a vulnerable contract, run the attacker test, and document your defensive choices for code reviewers.
